summary: Describes why the SIP 503 response is not enough for handling overload, when proxies and user agents lack resources to process requests, and lists requirements for a better mechanism. This is an informational document.

plainLanguage.summary: When SIP servers are overloaded, a 503 response can send requests bouncing among busy servers and create more work. RFC 5390 explains the problem and lists what a future overload-control mechanism should do.

questions: why sip 503 response is not enough
why is sip 503 not enough for overload
subtitle: Why SIP's 503 response is inadequate for overload control, and what a better mechanism needs.

tldr.problem: SIP's 503 response can cause extra retries, leave servers unused, and shift traffic all at once. It is also used for failures that do not mean the responding server is overloaded.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5390 describes these failure modes and sets requirements for an overload-control mechanism, including graded throttling, clear overload signals, stable behavior, and support for mixed deployments.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is a requirements document, not the overload-control protocol itself. It calls for preserving useful throughput and limiting cascading overload.

today: RFC 5390 is Informational and the supplied metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: How SIP Overload Starts
sections.content:
A SIP element is overloaded when it lacks the resources to process requests or responses. Relevant resources include processor time, memory, disk, I/O, and external services such as DNS or a database.

Overload can follow poor capacity planning, dependency or component failures, a burst of clients reconnecting, a flash crowd, or a denial-of-service attack. Delays and lost messages can trigger retransmissions, adding still more work to an already overloaded network.
sections.plainLanguage: A SIP server may become overloaded because it receives too much work or because a resource it depends on fails. Retries can increase the load when the server is already struggling.

sections.title: Why the 503 Response Can Backfire
sections.content:
A 503 response tells an upstream element that a server is temporarily unable to process a request. The upstream element may try another server, while a Retry-After value can tell it to pause requests to the rejecting server.

When several servers are overloaded, trying each in turn can multiply requests and responses, including retransmissions. A 503 may also be treated as applying to an entire hostname or server cluster, causing traffic to avoid healthy members. Retry-After is all-or-nothing and can move the full load between servers, creating unstable swings.
sections.plainLanguage: Retrying at another busy server can add more work without getting the request processed. Pausing all traffic to one server can also overload another server or leave capacity idle.

sections.title: Requirements for Overload Control
sections.content:
The RFC says a solution should preserve useful throughput, limit how one failure affects other elements, and work with both supporting and non-supporting elements. An explicit signal must identify overload rather than another failure, and an element must still function when it cannot send a signal.

Traffic reduction must be graded rather than all-or-nothing. The mechanism should avoid retrying on overloaded or unknown servers, allow requests to reach available servers, support local priorities such as emergency calls, work across domains and load balancers, and keep the system stable as offered load changes.
sections.plainLanguage: A useful solution reduces traffic gradually and makes clear why a server is rejecting work. It should preserve access to available servers, respect local priorities, and remain stable as conditions change.

sections.title: Security and Stability
sections.content:
An overload-control mechanism must account for malicious internal and external actors. A solution should not create a route for denial-of-service attacks or let an element claim overload to gain an unfair share of service.

The document also requires stability: once offered load falls below network capacity, throughput should stabilize and match that offered load. Load reporting may need to be restricted when an administrator considers it sensitive.
sections.plainLanguage: Overload signals must not let a malicious server mislead its neighbors or gain an unfair advantage. The network should settle back to normal behavior when the offered load falls.
